title: Address-decoder and read/write faults
summary: Not every fault sits in a cell. The **address decoder** can select the wrong cell, and the **read and write circuits** can disturb a cell while they access it. This topic covers these faults and the operations that catch them.
objectives: Describe the four address-decoder faults AF1–AF4 and the March condition that detects them.
Tell RDF, DRDF and IRF apart and explain why a DRDF needs two reads.
Explain write-disturb faults and how sense-amplifier and precharge faults appear to a test.

blocks.md: The row and column decoders turn an address into **one** selected word. A defect in a decoder gate breaks this one-to-one link. Seen from outside, only four things can go wrong — the four **address-decoder faults (AF)**:

steps.title: A good decoder
steps.md: Every address selects **exactly one** cell, and every cell is selected by **exactly one** address.

steps.title: AF1 — no cell
steps.md: An address selects **nothing**. A write to it is lost; a read returns a value that depends on the circuit (often the precharge level), not on the data written.

steps.title: AF2 — cell never reached
steps.md: A cell has **no address**. It can never be written or read; it behaves as if stuck at whatever it powered up with.

steps.title: AF3 — several cells
steps.md: One address selects **two or more cells** at once. A write goes into all of them; a read returns a mix of their values (often the AND or OR of them).

steps.title: AF4 — several addresses
steps.md: Two or more addresses select the **same cell**. Writing to one address overwrites what was written through the other.

blocks.title: They come in pairs
blocks.md: A single AF rarely appears alone. In a decoder with a fixed number of addresses and cells, a lost cell (AF2) usually goes with an address that selects nothing (AF1) or an address that selects two cells (AF3). In the last picture, AF4 on cell 3 also leaves cell 2 unreached — an AF2.

blocks.title: The March condition for address faults
blocks.md:
A test detects all AFs if it contains both

- **⇑(r x, …, w x̄)** — go **up** through the addresses, read the old value x, later write the opposite value, and
- **⇓(r x̄, …, w x)** — go **down**, read x̄, later write x back.

Example: **⇑(r0, w1) ⇓(r1, w0)**. When two addresses share a cell, the write through the *first* one is seen as a wrong value when the *second* one is read — in one direction or the other.

columns: Step (4 addresses, AF4: addresses 2 and 3 → cell 3)
blocks.caption: Going up, the write through address 2 is read back wrongly through address 3

blocks.md: A read is not completely harmless. During a read the bit lines are connected to the cell; a weak cell (for example with a too-small pull-down transistor) can be **flipped by its own read**. Three cases are distinguished, depending on **what the read returns** and **what the cell holds afterwards**:

steps.title: A good read
steps.md: The cell holds 0, **r0** returns 0, the cell still holds 0.

steps.title: RDF — read destructive fault
steps.md: The read **flips** the cell to 1 **and** returns the wrong value 1. Any read of the cell detects it.

steps.title: DRDF — deceptive read destructive fault
steps.md: The read returns the **correct** 0, but leaves the cell flipped to 1. The first read looks fine — only a **second read** of the same cell returns 1. A test needs **r0, r0** back to back.

steps.title: IRF — incorrect read fault
steps.md: The read returns the **wrong** value 1, but the cell is not changed. Usually a fault in the read path, not in the cell. One read detects it.

blocks.caption: Each fault exists for a cell holding 0 and for a cell holding 1

blocks.prompt: Practice: can a single read of the cell detect the fault?

blocks.md: Writes and the shared read circuitry can fail too. These faults look different from cell faults because they depend on the **operation** or affect a **whole column**:

rows: A **non-transition** write (w0 into a cell that holds 0) flips the cell to 1.
Write the same value twice or write x into a cell already holding x, then read: **w0, r0**.
The sense amplifier of one column always decides 0 (or 1), or is too slow.
Every cell of that **column** reads stuck at one value — looks like many stuck-at faults in one column.
A bit line is not fully precharged before a read.
The read result depends on the **previous** access in that column; seen as wrong reads after a read of the opposite value.
After a write, the bit lines are not restored in time.
A read right **after a write** of the opposite value in the same column fails; needs at-speed back-to-back operations.
blocks.caption: Faults in the write path and in the shared read circuits

blocks.title: Why this matters for MBIST
blocks.md: These faults explain several features of real March tests and MBIST hardware: **back-to-back reads** (DRDF), **non-transition writes** (WDF), **both address directions** (AF) and running at **full clock speed** (recovery and precharge faults). Topic 7 puts all of them into one notation.
